setup: Model 1 (no drift), $dr = \sigma\,dw$. The short rate is 6.18% and the annual basis-point volatility is $\sigma = 113$ bp. The tree steps monthly, $dt = 1/12$.
ask: The standard deviation of the one-month rate change is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 9.4 bp
options.why: Scaled by $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$: $113/12$. Volatility scales with the square root of time.

options.label: ≈ 113 bp
options.why: The annual volatility, never scaled down to one month.

options.label: ≈ 390 bp
options.why: Multiplied by $\sqrt{12}$ instead of dividing: that goes from monthly to annual, not the other way.

takeaway: A one-month step carries about 0.29× the annual bp vol ($\sqrt{1/12}$), so a monthly move is roughly a third of $\sigma$.

setup: Model 1 (no drift), $dr = \sigma\,dw$. The rate starts at 6%. Annual volatility is $\sigma = 1.20\%$ and the step is one month. The drawn shock is $dw = 0.2$; $dw$ already has standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.
ask: The one-month rate change is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 2.4 bp
options.why: Percent-to-bp slip: $0.24\%$ is 24 bp, not 2.4 bp.

options.label: ≈ 6.9 bp
options.why: Multiplied by $\sqrt{1/12}$ a second time. The $\sqrt{dt}$ is already inside $dw$.

options.label: ≈ 120 bp
options.why: Took the full annual $\sigma$ and never multiplied by the drawn $dw$.

working.label: In basis points
working.display: $0.24\% = 24$ bp, so the new rate is $6.24\%$

takeaway: In $dr = \sigma\,dw$ the time scaling lives inside $dw$. Don't apply $\sqrt{dt}$ twice.

setup: Vasicek: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\,dw$. $k = 0.03$, current rate $r = 6.2\%$, long-run level $\theta = 18\%$, one-month step.
ask: The expected (drift-only) rate change over the month is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.89 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3× the true drift).

options.label: ≈ 35 bp
options.why: Left out $dt$: $0.03 \times 11.8\% = 0.354\%$ is the annual drift, not the monthly one.

options.label: ≈ 98 bp
options.why: Left out $k$: $11.8\% / 12$ assumes the gap closes at full speed.

takeaway: With $k = 0.03$ only 3% of the gap closes per year, and a month is 1/12 of that: a few bp.

setup: Monthly Vasicek tree: $k = 0.03$, $\theta = 18\%$, $\sigma = 150$ bp, so each shock is $\pm 1.5\%/\sqrt{12} = \pm 0.433\%$. The date-1 nodes are 6.663% (up) and 5.796% (down). The drift $k(\theta - r)\,dt$ is recomputed at each node.
ask: At date 2, which middle node is higher: up-then-down or down-then-up?

options.label: Up-then-down
options.why: The two shocks cancel on both paths, so only the drift differs. The drift is larger from the lower node (5.796%), which is farther below $\theta$.

options.label: Identical: the tree recombines
options.why: That holds for Model 1, Model 2 and Ho-Lee. The Vasicek drift depends on the current rate, so the two paths land about 0.2 bp apart.

takeaway: Mean reversion pulls harder from the lower node, so the Vasicek tree doesn't recombine until you average the middle nodes.

setup: Vasicek: $r_0 = 6.2\%$, $\theta = 18\%$, $k = 0.03$. Halfway from 6.2% to 18% is 12.1%.
ask: The expected short rate in 10 years is above 12.1%, below it, or at roughly 12.1%?

options.label: Above 12.1%
options.why: That would need $T$ beyond the 23.1-year half-life. At $T = 10$, $e^{-0.3} = 0.74$ of the gap is still open.

options.label: Roughly 12.1%
options.why: The rate reaches the halfway level only at $T \approx 23.1$ years, not at 10.

takeaway: Before one half-life, less than half the gap to $\theta$ has closed: $E[r_T] = \theta - (\theta - r_0)e^{-kT}$.

setup: Gaussian copula. One-year cumulative default probabilities: company B 6.51%, company Caa 23.83%. Their standard-normal percentiles are $-1.5133$ and $-0.7118$. One-year Gaussian default correlation is $\rho = 0.4$. If the two were independent, the joint probability would be $6.51\% \times 23.83\% = 1.55\%$.
ask: Compared with 1.55%, the copula's joint one-year default probability is higher, lower, or about the same?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Positive correlation makes the two thresholds tend to be breached together, so joint default is more likely than under independence, not less.

options.label: About the same
options.why: At $\rho = 0.4$ the bivariate normal gives 3.44%, more than double the independent 1.55%.

takeaway: Positive default correlation pushes the joint probability above the product of the marginals, but never above the smaller marginal.

setup: Step 1 of the Gaussian default-time copula maps each cumulative default probability to a standard-normal percentile, $N^{-1}(Q)$. Company B has $Q_B(3) = 21.03\%$. Company Caa has $Q_{Caa}(5) = 60.09\%$.
ask: What are the signs of the two percentiles?

options.label: Both negative
options.why: Default thresholds aren't always negative. Any $Q$ above 50% sits above the median of the standard normal, so its percentile is positive.

options.label: Both positive
options.why: Probabilities are positive, but a percentile is a z-value: any $Q$ below 50% maps to a negative $z$.

takeaway: $N^{-1}(Q)$ is negative below 50% and positive above it. The 50% line is the sign switch.

setup: Correlated default time: set the sampled copula value equal to B's cumulative default probability, $M_n(\bullet) = Q_B(\tau)$, and solve for $\tau$. B's curve: 21.03% at year 3, 27.04% at year 4, 36.73% at year 6, 40.97% at year 7. A draw of 0.24 gives $\tau \approx 3.5$ years.
ask: If the draw had been 0.40 instead, the implied default time would be later, earlier, or unchanged?

options.label: Earlier
options.why: A bigger draw sounds like more default risk, but $Q_B$ is cumulative and rising, so a higher level is reached further out on the curve.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The draw is the level you enter the curve at; a different level lands on a different year.

takeaway: The cumulative default curve only rises, so a larger draw maps to a later default time.

setup: An active manager expects an information ratio of 0.5 and targets 5% active risk. Active risk aversion is backed out as $\lambda_A = \text{IR}/(2\sigma_A)$, with $\sigma_A$ entered in percent.
ask: $\lambda_A$ is closest to:

options.why: Used the variance: $0.5/(2 \times 25)$. The formula takes $\sigma_A$, not $\sigma_A^2$.
Divided by 2 but dropped $\sigma_A$.
Entered $\sigma_A$ as the decimal 0.05. The optimizer expects percent.

takeaway: $\lambda_A = \text{IR}/(2\sigma_A)$ with $\sigma_A$ in percent: IR 0.5 and 5% gives 0.05.

setup: Rebalancing with transaction costs: purchase cost $\text{PC}_n = 0.50\%$, sales cost $\text{SC}_n = 0.75\%$. New information moves a stock's marginal contribution to value added to $\text{MCVA}_n = -0.60\%$.
ask: What should the manager do with this stock?

options.label: Sell some
options.why: Used a symmetric $\pm 0.50\%$ band. The lower edge is $-\text{SC}_n = -0.75\%$, and $-0.60\%$ is inside it.

options.label: Buy more
options.why: Sign flip: a negative MCVA never argues for buying. The buy trigger is MCVA above $+0.50\%$.

working.label: Room above the sell edge
working.display: $-0.60\% - (-0.75\%) = +0.15\%$, so MCVA is inside the band

takeaway: Trade only when MCVA leaves $[-\text{SC},\ +\text{PC}]$. The band is asymmetric when the two costs differ.

setup: No-trade band with purchase cost 0.50% and sales cost 0.75%. Stock 1 has $\text{MCVA} = +0.80\%$; stock 2 has $\text{MCVA} = -1.30\%$. Both sit outside the band.
ask: Which trade has the larger net benefit at the margin: buying stock 1 or selling stock 2?

options.label: Buying stock 1
options.why: Sign slip: $-1.30 + 0.75 = -0.55$ reads like a loss. For a sale, the benefit is the 1.30% of value you stop losing, minus the 0.75% cost: $+0.55\%$.

takeaway: Net benefit of a trade is how far MCVA sits beyond its own edge of the band: $|\text{MCVA}|$ minus that side's cost.

setup: A USD 500m position in W has volatility 10%. The manager will add USD 500m of either X (volatility 9%, correlation with W 0.7) or Y (volatility 12%, correlation with W 0). Either way the result is a 50/50 mix.
ask: Which mix has the higher return volatility: W+X or W+Y?

options.label: W+Y
options.why: Picked the asset with the higher standalone vol. With zero correlation the cross term vanishes, so W+Y comes out at 7.81%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: 8.76% against 7.81% is nearly a full point apart. The 0.7 correlation is what separates them.

takeaway: Standalone volatility doesn't decide the addition; correlation does. The 12% asset at $\rho = 0$ adds less risk than the 9% asset at $\rho = 0.7$.

setup: W alone: USD 500m at 10% volatility, so 99% VaR is $2.33 \times 10\% \times 500 = $ USD 116.5m. The manager adds USD 500m of Y (volatility 12%, correlation 0 with W), which cuts portfolio return volatility to 7.81%.
ask: Dollar VaR after adding Y rises, falls, or stays roughly the same?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Return volatility fell, but the portfolio doubled to USD 1,000m. Keeping USD 500m in the VaR step gives USD 91m, the standard slip.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: USD 182m against USD 116.5m is a rise of more than 50%.

takeaway: Lower return volatility on a bigger book can still mean a bigger dollar VaR. Scale by the new portfolio size.

setup: A USD 525m fund allocates USD 194m to manager 2, whose tracking-error volatility (TEV) is 6%. Each manager's risk budget is the 99% VaR of their tracking error, with $z = 2.33$.
ask: Manager 2's risk budget is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.6m
options.why: Used the variance ($0.06^2$) in place of the TEV.

options.label: ≈ USD 73m
options.why: Applied the manager's TEV to the whole USD 525m fund instead of the USD 194m allocated.

options.label: ≈ USD 450m
options.why: Dropped the TEV. $2.33 \times 194$ treats the full allocation as the risk, not the deviation from the benchmark.

takeaway: Active risk budget = $z \times$ TEV $\times$ the capital the manager actually runs.

setup: Two active managers with independent tracking errors: IRs 0.60 and 0.40, each with TEV 6%. Weights are set in proportion to IR to hit a 4% fund TEV: 55.5% and 37.0%, with the rest in the benchmark. Expected excess return is $0.555 \times 3.6\% + 0.370 \times 2.4\%$.
ask: Compared with the better manager's 0.60, the fund's information ratio is above, below, or equal?

options.label: Below 0.60
options.why: Averaged the two IRs to about 0.5. Independent active risks diversify, so the combined IR is $\sqrt{0.6^2 + 0.4^2} = 0.72$.

options.label: Equal to 0.60
options.why: That would mean manager 2 adds nothing. Because the two tracking errors are independent, manager 2 still lifts the combined IR.

takeaway: With independent tracking errors and IR-proportional risk budgets, $\text{IR}_p = \sqrt{\sum \text{IR}_i^2}$, above every single manager.

setup: Gauss+: the short-term factor follows $dr_t = -\alpha_r (r_t - m_t)\,dt$, with no shock term. Today $r = 2.00\%$, $m = 3.00\%$, $\alpha_r = 1.0547$, $dt = 1/12$. This month's shocks are $dW^1 = 0.10$ and $dW^2 = -0.05$.
ask: Over the month, the short-term factor rises, falls, or stays unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Dropped the leading minus: $-1.0547 \times (2\% - 3\%)$ is positive. $r$ is below $m$, so it's pulled up.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: No shock doesn't mean no move. The drift alone pulls $r$ toward $m$, and neither $dW$ enters $dr$.

takeaway: In Gauss+, $r$ is pure drift toward $m$: below $m$ it rises, above $m$ it falls.

setup: Gauss+ medium-term factor over one month. The drift $-\alpha_m(m - l)\,dt$, with $\alpha_m = 0.6358$, $m = 3\%$, $l = 4\%$, comes to $+0.0530\%$. The shock is $\sigma_m[\rho\,dW^1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,dW^2]$ with $\sigma_m = 1.092\%$, $\rho = 0.212$, $dW^1 = 0.10$, $dW^2 = -0.05$.
ask: Is the net change $dm$ positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Gave $dW^2$ full weight and dropped the $\rho\,dW^1$ term: $1.092\% \times (-0.05) = -0.055\%$. With both terms weighted, the shock is only $-0.030\%$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The shock ($-0.030\%$) offsets under 60% of the drift ($+0.053\%$). A net $+2.3$ bp is clear.

takeaway: In $dm$ both shocks are weighted, $\rho$ and $\sqrt{1-\rho^2}$. Size the shock before you assume it swamps the drift.

setup: Gauss+ long-term factor: $dl = -\alpha_l(l - \mu)\,dt + \sigma_l\,dW^1$. $\alpha_l = 0.0165$, $l = 4.00\%$, $\mu = 10.555\%$, $\sigma_l = 96.4$ bp, $dt = 1/12$, $dW^1 = 0.10$.
ask: The one-month change in $l$ is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.90 bp
options.why: Drift only. Slow mean reversion makes the drift tiny, but the shock $\sigma_l\,dW^1$ still applies.

options.label: ≈ 3.2 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3× the true change).

options.label: ≈ 97 bp
options.why: Added the full $\sigma_l$ without multiplying by the realized $dW^1 = 0.10$.

takeaway: The slowest-reverting factor can make the biggest move: its drift is under 1 bp, but its shock isn't.

setup: One month in Gauss+: $r = 2\%$, $m = 3\%$, $l = 4\%$, $\mu = 10.555\%$, $dt = 1/12$. $\alpha_r = 1.0547$ (half-life 0.66 yr), $\alpha_l = 0.0165$ (half-life 42 yr). $r$ has no shock; $l$ gets $\sigma_l\,dW^1 = 96.4\text{ bp} \times 0.10$.
ask: Which factor moves more this month: $r$ or $l$?

options.label: $r$
options.why: Fast mean reversion doesn't guarantee a big move. $r$ is only 1% from $m$, so $dr \approx 8.8$ bp, while $l$'s shock alone is 9.6 bp.

options.label: Neither moves more than 1 bp
options.why: That's the size of $l$'s drift alone. Both $dr$ (8.8 bp) and the $l$ shock (9.6 bp) are far larger.

takeaway: Slow mean reversion doesn't mean a small move. It means the factor isn't pulled back quickly once it moves.

setup: Buy one share at 50. At year end it pays a 2 dividend and is worth 53 (year-1 return 10.00%). Buy a second share at 53. In year 2 both pay 2 and are sold at 54 (year-2 return 5.66%). The time-weighted (geometric) return is 7.81%.
ask: The dollar-weighted return (IRR) is above, below, or equal to 7.81%?

options.label: Above 7.81%
options.why: More money was at work in year 2, the weaker year (5.66%), so the IRR is pulled toward it, not toward 10%.

options.label: Equal to 7.81%
options.why: They match only when no money is added or withdrawn mid-horizon. Here a second share was bought.

takeaway: The dollar-weighted return leans toward the periods with the most money invested. Here that is the weaker year, so it is lower.

setup: To test a manager's alpha, $t = \alpha / (\sigma/\sqrt{N})$, where $\sigma$ should be the standard deviation of the regression residuals (the tracking error). An analyst uses the portfolio's total return volatility for $\sigma$ instead.
ask: Relative to the correct figure, the analyst's t-statistic is too large, too small, or unaffected?

options.label: Too large
options.why: Total volatility includes the market-driven part, so it is at least as big as the residual s.d. A bigger denominator shrinks $t$.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: $\sigma$ sits in the denominator, so a bigger $\sigma$ gives a proportionally smaller $t$.

working.label: Which $\sigma$
working.display: Total vol $\ge$ residual vol, because it adds the systematic part

working.label: Effect on $t$
working.display: Bigger denominator $\Rightarrow$ smaller $t$: the manager looks insignificant when she may not be

takeaway: Use the residual s.d. in the alpha t-test. Total volatility understates $t$.
